title: A Volumetric Anatomy-Aware, Prompt-Guided Adaptation Framework for the Segment Anything Model in Head and Neck Radiotherapy.
abstract: Background Head and neck (H&N) radiotherapy planning requires accurate segmentation of numerous organs at risk (OARs), yet many critical structures, such as the optic nerves, chiasm, and cochleae, are small, poorly contrasted on CT, and prone to high inter-observer variability in manual contouring. Recent foundation models like Segment Anything Model (SAM) and its 3D medical variants (SAM-Med3D) offer prompt-based, interactive segmentation, but their real-world utility for H&N small OARs is hindered by unreliable prompt sources and unstable performance on fine anatomical targets. To address these issues, this work proposes an anatomy-aware prompt generation and prompt-guided adaptation tailored specifically for small-structure segmentation to improve both precision and automation feasibility. Purpose To address these challenges, we developed a domain-adapted framework, SAM-FT-HN, by fine-tuning a volumetric SAM backbone (SAM-Med3D) for automated delineation of H&N OARs in radiotherapy planning. Our approach incorporates a coarse-to-fine pipeline in which a lightweight localization network automatically generates organ-specific prompts and candidate regions, followed by a fine-tuned volumetric SAM backbone for refinement. We further introduced task-specific strategies including region-of-interest (ROI)-guided tiny-organ enhancement and organ-specific threshold calibration to improve performance on small structures. The primary objective is to develop and evaluate a fully automated, anatomy-aware adaptation of SAM-Med3D for H&N OAR segmentation, with a secondary objective of improving small-organ segmentation. We systematically compared SAM-FT-HN against baseline SAM-Med3D and nnUNet models quantitatively and qualitatively. Methods We used an institutional H&N CT dataset of 211 patients with manual delineations of 23 OARs, standardized for training, validation, and testing. Eighty percent of cases were used for training and validation, and twenty percent for testing. The testing phase used CT volumes only, and ground-truth masks were used solely for metric calculation. A coarse localization network was trained to generate automatic prompts and ROI candidates. SAM-FT-HN was fine-tuned using task-specific adaptations, and small-organ refinement was performed using ROI-guided enhancement and organ-specific threshold calibration. nnUNet was trained using its automated configuration pipeline. Performance was evaluated using overlap and boundary metrics. Results For large OARs, SAM-FT-HN achieved a mean Dice of 0.814 compared with 0.791 for nnUNet and substantially higher than SAM-Med3D (0.609). For small organs, SAM-FT-HN improved the mean Dice from 0.300 to 0.669 compared with SAM-Med3D and reduced HD95 by approximately 65%, although nnUNet remained higher in average small-organ Dice (0.720). Overall, across all organs, SAM-FT-HN achieved a mean Dice score of 0.770, compared with 0.769 for nnUNet. Overall, SAM-FT-HN showed no statistically significant difference from nnUNet in the patient-level analysis, while substantially outperforming the original SAM-Med3D baseline. Conclusion Fine-tuning a foundation model with anatomy-aware automatic prompting, coarse-to-fine localization, and adaptive thresholding markedly improves small-organ segmentation, substantially mitigating a key limitation of the original foundation model. SAM-FT-HN offers a competitive approach for H&N radiotherapy contouring, with potential for future adaptive workflows.

title: Epidermoid Cyst of the Cecum: A Case Report of an Exceptionally Rare Entity and Review of the Literature.
abstract: Epidermoid cysts of the cecum are extremely rare benign lesions of the gastrointestinal tract. Their diagnosis remains challenging due to the lack of specific clinical symptoms and inconclusive radiological findings. Consequently, accurate preoperative diagnosis is difficult, with lesions often being misdiagnosed as appendiceal mucoceles, gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs), duplication cysts, or adnexal masses. We report the case of a 59-year-old male who presented with right lower quadrant abdominal pain and a palpable mass. Comprehensive diagnostic imaging, including abdominal ultrasonography, abdominopelvic computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), revealed a well-circumscribed cystic lesion arising from the cecal wall, initially concerning for a cecal neoplasm or appendiceal mucocele. The patient underwent a successful right hemicolectomy, and histopathological examination definitively confirmed a cecal epidermoid cyst lined by stratified squamous epithelium containing keratinaceous debris. Postoperative recovery was uneventful. Although exceptionally rare, epidermoid cysts should be included in the differential diagnosis of right lower quadrant masses. Despite the limited number of reported cases, complete surgical excision remains the definitive treatment of choice, providing an excellent long-term prognosis with no evidence of recurrence.

title: Multilevel Lumbar Epidural Angiolipoma: A Case Report.
abstract: Spinal angiolipomas are rare benign tumors composed of mature adipose tissue and vascular elements, most commonly located in the thoracic epidural space. Lumbar involvement is considerably less frequent, and variable proportions of adipose and vascular tissue may result in atypical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) characteristics and diagnostic uncertainty. We report the case of a 36-year-old woman with an approximately one-year history of persistent low back pain associated with subjective bilateral lower-extremity weakness despite a preserved neurological examination. An initial non-contrast lumbar MRI was interpreted as showing no significant abnormality other than minimal degenerative changes; however, retrospective review revealed a subtle posterior epidural lesion. Because of persistent symptoms, further investigation with contrast-enhanced MRI was performed, demonstrating an elongated epidural lesion extending from L1 to L3, predominantly involving the posterior and right posterolateral epidural space with associated foraminal extension. The lesion demonstrated areas of low T1 signal intensity and intense homogeneous contrast enhancement. The patient underwent L1-L3 laminoplasty and gross-total resection. Intraoperatively, the lesion had a macroscopically adipose appearance and was moderately vascular. Histopathological examination demonstrated mature adipose tissue admixed with numerous vascular channels, confirming the diagnosis of spinal angiolipoma. Postoperatively, pain and subjective lower-extremity weakness improved without new neurological deficits, and early postoperative MRI showed no evidence of residual or recurrent tumor. This case highlights the variable imaging appearance of lumbar spinal angiolipomas and the value of correlating MRI characteristics with intraoperative and histopathological findings, particularly in enhancing epidural lesions without a predominantly fatty appearance.

title: Individualized Positive End-Expiratory Pressure and Postoperative Pulmonary Outcomes in Laparoscopic and Robotic Abdominal-Pelvic Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Postoperative pulmonary complications remain clinically important after laparoscopic and robot-assisted abdominal-pelvic surgery, where pneumoperitoneum, altered respiratory mechanics, obesity, and procedure-specific positioning can promote lung collapse. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated whether individualized intraoperative positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), selected using patient-specific physiological or imaging responses, improves postoperative pulmonary outcomes compared with fixed or conventional PEEP. Randomized controlled trials involving adults undergoing eligible minimally invasive abdominal-pelvic procedures were identified through PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar and were included when they reported postoperative pulmonary or direct lung-aeration outcomes after extubation. Data were synthesized narratively, with random-effects meta-analysis performed for clinically compatible outcomes, and methodological quality was evaluated using a Cochrane risk-of-bias framework. Across the included evidence, individualized PEEP was generally associated with fewer postoperative pulmonary complications, fewer early postoperative oxygenation problems, and better postoperative lung-aeration measures, whereas binary atelectasis outcomes were more heterogeneous. Favorable findings were observed across driving-pressure-, compliance-, electrical-impedance-tomography-, and lung-ultrasound-guided approaches, although variation in outcome definitions, assessment times, and trial methods limits conclusions regarding the optimal titration strategy. Current evidence suggests that patient-specific PEEP selection may improve postoperative pulmonary outcomes, although larger, standardized trials are needed to determine the most effective titration strategy.

title: Neonatal Immature Retroperitoneal Teratoma With Pancreatic Involvement and Intraoperative Findings Mimicking Fetus in Fetu.
abstract: Retroperitoneal teratomas are uncommon pediatric germ cell tumors and are exceptional during the neonatal period. Their diagnosis and treatment are challenging because they may compress major abdominal vessels and involve adjacent organs. We report the case of a two-day-old male neonate who presented with progressive abdominal distension and a palpable abdominal mass. Ultrasonography and computed tomography demonstrated a 9 × 9 cm heterogeneous retroperitoneal lesion with solid, cystic, and calcified components, associated with displacement of bowel loops, compression of major vessels, and apparent pancreatic involvement. Exploratory laparotomy with tumor resection was performed. Intraoperatively, the lesion showed macroscopic structures resembling a hand and a foot, raising the differential diagnosis of fetus in fetu. The pancreatic tail was considered involved intraoperatively and was resected, while the pancreatic head and body were preserved. Histopathological examination confirmed a grade 3 extragonadal immature teratoma with no vertebral axis. The pathology report also described partial pancreatic tail involvement; however, the available pathology documentation did not further characterize the pancreatic-tumor interface or the pancreatic resection margin. The postoperative hospital course was favorable, although prolonged neonatal intensive care was required. This case highlights the importance of preoperative imaging, careful retroperitoneal dissection, vascular control, patient-specific clarification of distorted anatomy, and histopathological confirmation when evaluating complex neonatal abdominal masses.

title: Abdominal Pannus Delays Detection of Abdominal Wall Abscess.
abstract: Abdominal wall abscesses (AWA) of primary etiology are rare, typically presenting in the context of atypical infections or in the setting of immunocompromise. Development of such pathology typically occurs only in the context of subclinical infections or severe systemic or metabolic disease. AWA more frequently develops as a secondary process due to underlying abdominal pathology such as chronic inflammatory conditions. In non-obese patients, AWA is often more readily apparent on exam with abnormalities of the abdominal contour, lending to prompt diagnosis and treatment, and even in those who are overweight, symptoms typically precede diagnosis as imaging is sought to delineate etiology. Herein, we present the case of an 82-year-old, morbidly obese man with a known history of atrial fibrillation who presented for three days of mild pain and drainage from a purported spider bite to the right lower quadrant of the abdomen, located along a distended pannus that had itself reportedly been present for 10 years. Initial examination showed firmness and swelling of the pannus and purulent drainage with minimal erythema surrounding a <1 cm lesion. Labs demonstrated leukocytosis with a WBC of 19.2 x 10 3 /μL and subsequent computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis showed a complex fluid collection in the subcutaneous soft tissue of the abdominal wall, 36.5 x 11.1 x 18.3 cm, consistent with AWA. Infectious management was initiated with broad-spectrum antibiotics, and he was taken for incision and drainage (I&D) once medically stable, with intraoperative findings confirming the AWA with surrounding rind, which was excised with subsequent washout and wound vac placement. The patient's clinical course was further complicated by recurrence of atrial fibrillation with BPM in the 110-130s range and subsequent discovery of a 5 mm mitral valve vegetation on transesophageal echocardiogram. Wound cultures grew Bacteroides fragilis and Aeromonas hydrophila while blood cultures, in contrast, grew Streptococcus mitis . With treatment of both his AWA and newly discovered mitral valve endocarditis, the patient improved and was eventually discharged from the hospital following confirmation of persistently negative blood cultures. Primary AWA is a rare condition, and this report highlights a case which likely avoided detection for multiple years due to the patient's obese body habitus. The case strengthens the convention of treatment for primary AWA with combined surgical and antibiotic interventions and also highlights the need for extensive culture data to best characterize sources of infection in remote bodily sites. Overall, this helps to not only delineate treatment methods for a primary process, but to emphasize the importance of thorough, guided workup of an infectious process.

title: Changes in Training Quality and Workload Among Radiology Trainees Pre- and Post-COVID-19 Pandemic: A Systematic Review.
abstract: This review aimed to systematically review changes in radiology trainee training quality and workload before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic, assessing its impact on educational experiences, clinical and procedural exposure, workload demands, trainee wellbeing, and the adoption of adaptive educational strategies such as virtual learning and simulation-based training. A systematic review was performed following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Electronic databases, including PubMed, Elsevier ScienceDirect and Web of Science, were searched for studies evaluating the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on radiology trainee workload, education, and training quality. Supplementary searches of Google Scholar and relevant professional organisation websites, including the Royal College of Radiologists, were conducted, alongside targeted searches of Clinical Radiology and other relevant radiology publications. Although studies from multiple countries were included, findings were interpreted in the context of the UK radiology training curriculum and changes to radiology training and service provision during the COVID-19 pandemic. Eligible studies were analysed using narrative synthesis. The COVID-19 pandemic significantly affected radiology trainee workload and training quality across multiple domains. Common findings included reduced clinical exposure, decreased reporting opportunities, loss of face-to-face teaching, reduced procedural experience, and concerns regarding competency attainment. Imaging volumes declined substantially because of the postponement of elective imaging and outpatient services, resulting in reduced exposure to radiographs, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), ultrasound, and interventional radiology procedures. Training progression was further affected by examination delays, rota disruptions, redeployment, and reduced consultant supervision. Increased psychological burden, including stress, anxiety, and burnout, was also reported across multiple studies. Despite these challenges, radiology training programmes demonstrated adaptability through the rapid adoption of virtual learning, remote reporting, simulation-based teaching, and digital educational platforms, improving accessibility and flexibility. These adaptations contributed to the development of increasingly hybrid training models combining virtual and face-to-face learning. The COVID-19 pandemic substantially disrupted radiology trainee workload, training quality, clinical exposure, and procedural experience. However, it also accelerated the adoption of virtual learning, digital platforms, remote working, and simulation-based education. The post-pandemic period has therefore seen continued integration of these approaches alongside traditional apprenticeship-based training, with potential implications for the future delivery of radiology education and training.

title: Beyond Sinonasal Undifferentiated Carcinoma: Molecular Reclassification of a SMARCB1-Deficient Sinonasal Carcinoma With Pulmonary Metastasis.
abstract: A 56-year-old man presented with a nine-month history of progressive left-sided nasal obstruction, epistaxis, facial and palatal pain, and proptosis. Imaging demonstrated a large destructive left sinonasal mass extending into the left maxillary sinus and orbit. An endoscopic biopsy revealed a poorly differentiated epithelial malignancy, initially classified as a sinonasal undifferentiated carcinoma (SNUC). Immunohistochemistry demonstrated strong cytokeratin expression and complete loss of integrase interactor 1 (INI1) nuclear expression in tumor cells, with retained staining in non-neoplastic elements. The patient underwent a left subtotal maxillectomy with hard palate resection. The tumor measured at least 8 cm, involved the pterygoid muscle, and extended to the medial and superior resection margins. Following surgery, he received platinum-based chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Approximately two years later, he presented with progressive exertional dyspnea. Imaging revealed a large left pleural effusion and bilateral soft-tissue-attenuation pulmonary nodules. Pleural fluid evaluation was nondiagnostic for malignancy because of limited cellularity; however, a computed tomography-guided core biopsy of a right pulmonary nodule revealed metastatic carcinoma morphologically concordant with the sinonasal primary, with strong cytokeratin expression and persistent loss of INI1. The patient subsequently received six cycles of pembrolizumab combined with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and vincristine. Comprehensive molecular profiling of archived primary tumor tissue later identified a pathogenic SMARCB1 copy-number deletion, establishing the diagnosis of SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma. At the last documented follow-up, fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) demonstrated persistent metabolically active thoracic metastatic disease without interval progression or new sites of disease. This case illustrates how integration of morphology, immunohistochemistry, metastatic-site comparison, and molecular testing can refine the classification of a poorly differentiated sinonasal carcinoma initially diagnosed as SNUC.

title: Histomorphological Renal Changes in the Offspring of Streptozotocin-Induced Diabetic Wistar Rats.
abstract: Introduction Maternal diabetes mellitus can adversely affect fetal development and may predispose offspring to metabolic and renal abnormalities. However, early renal structural changes following intrauterine exposure to maternal hyperglycemia remain incompletely characterized. This study evaluated the metabolic and histomorphological effects of maternal diabetes on rat offspring kidneys during the early postnatal period. Methods This experimental study was conducted using Wistar rats. Diabetes was induced in female rats using streptozotocin before mating. We evaluated offspring of diabetic and nondiabetic mothers during the first and second postnatal weeks. We assessed blood glucose levels and relative kidney weights. Kidney tissues were processed routinely for histopathology. We used hematoxylin and eosin, Masson's trichrome, and periodic acid-Schiff stains to evaluate histopathological changes. Renal morphometric parameters, including glomerular diameter and Bowman's space, were assessed using computer-assisted digital morphometry. Results Offspring of diabetic mothers showed significantly higher blood glucose levels during both the first and second postnatal weeks compared with controls. Relative kidney weight was also higher in the test group at both time points. Histopathological examination demonstrated focal interstitial lymphocytic infiltration in the cortex and medulla during the first postnatal week, which became more prominent during the second week. Mild cortical tubular atrophy and early interstitial fibrosis with minimal collagen deposition were observed during the second week. Morphometric analysis showed significantly increased glomerular diameter and reduced Bowman's space in the test group compared with controls during both postnatal weeks (p < 0.001). Conclusion Maternal diabetes was associated with persistent hyperglycemia, increased relative kidney weight, and early structural alterations in the kidneys of rat offspring. The progressive inflammatory, tubular, fibrotic, and glomerular changes observed during the early postnatal period suggest that maternal hyperglycemia may adversely influence renal development and potentially increase susceptibility to later-life renal complications.

title: Appendiceal Hydatid Disease Presenting as Acute Appendicitis: A Case Report and Review of the Literature.
abstract: Appendiceal hydatid disease is an exceptionally rare manifestation of cystic echinococcosis and may be indistinguishable from routine acute appendicitis before surgery. We report a 43-year-old man who presented with a two-day history of right lower-quadrant abdominal pain, anorexia, and nausea. Clinical examination demonstrated localized tenderness at McBurney's point with signs of localized peritoneal irritation. Laboratory investigations showed leukocytosis and an elevated C-reactive protein level. Abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated a non-compressible, inflamed appendix measuring approximately 9 mm in diameter with a fecalith-like intraluminal structure, and emergency open appendectomy was undertaken for presumed acute appendicitis. Intraoperatively, an unexpected cystic lesion was identified adjacent to the appendiceal base and ruptured during dissection, with extrusion of whitish membrane-like material. The operative field was immediately irrigated with hypertonic saline, and no intraoperative anaphylactic reaction occurred. Histopathological examination demonstrated laminated and germinal layers consistent with cystic echinococcosis. The patient subsequently received albendazole 400 mg twice daily in three 28-day cycles separated by 14-day treatment-free intervals. Follow-up computed tomography performed three months after surgery demonstrated no residual or additional hydatid cysts at that time, and the patient remained clinically well without evidence of recurrence during 12 months of follow-up. This case, considered alongside the published literature, highlights the diagnostic difficulty of appendiceal hydatid disease, the importance of cautious handling of unexpected cystic appendiceal lesions, and the need for postoperative antiparasitic treatment and imaging surveillance.

title: Fever and Painful Skin Lesions: When to Consider Sweet's Syndrome.
abstract: Sweet's syndrome is an acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis characterised by fever, neutrophilia, and painful cutaneous lesions. We describe a case of a 31-year-old male admitted with a two-week history of fever up to 39°C and painful erythematous papules, scattered and coalescing into plaques over the trunk and limbs, together with pustules on an erythematous base over the palms and dorsum of the hands. No relevant epidemiological exposure or recent drug exposure was identified. Investigation showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 40 mm/h, leucocytosis of 14,380/µL with 77% neutrophils and no eosinophilia, and a C-reactive protein of 1.21 mg/dL. Liver and renal function, albumin, lactate dehydrogenase, serum iron, ferritin, and serum protein electrophoresis were normal, and a respiratory viral panel was negative. Blood, urine, and pustule cultures, an interferon-gamma release assay, and serology for human immunodeficiency virus, syphilis, hepatitis A, B, C, and E viruses, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein-Barr virus were negative, as was an autoantibody panel. Serum immunoglobulin A was below the detection limit (<0.07 g/L) before corticosteroid therapy and on all repeat measurements, including after treatment had been discontinued, with normal immunoglobulin G and M, and IgG-based coeliac serology was negative. Computed tomography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and peripheral blood immunophenotyping showed no abnormalities. A skin biopsy demonstrated intraepidermal blisters and a superficial perivascular neutrophilic infiltrate without vasculitis, spongiform pustules, or psoriasiform changes. The clinical and laboratory criteria for classical Sweet's syndrome were fulfilled, and the histology was compatible with, although not classical for, the syndrome. Prednisolone 60 mg/day (approximately 0.6 mg/kg/day) was started on clinical suspicion of the syndrome. After one week, the fever had resolved, but the lesions worsened slightly, prompting escalation to 100 mg/day (approximately 1 mg/kg/day), after which they regressed progressively and resolved completely within three weeks of dose escalation, with normalisation of the leucocyte count. Corticosteroids were tapered and discontinued before the three-month assessment, at which there was no relapse and no evidence of malignancy. This case illustrates three practical points: an acral pustular morphology does not exclude the diagnosis; early worsening under corticosteroid therapy may reflect an initial dose insufficient for body weight rather than an incorrect diagnosis, once infection has been rigorously excluded; and the coexisting finding of selective immunoglobulin A deficiency carries independent implications for coeliac disease screening and long-term follow-up.

title: Pathobiology and Precision Management of Benign and Malignant Bone Tumors: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Bone tumors range from incidental benign lesions and locally aggressive intermediate tumors to primary sarcomas, and metastatic carcinoma is the most common malignant lesion of adult bone. This narrative review focuses on primary bone tumors, examining their classification, molecular pathobiology, diagnosis, staging, and treatment, and it addresses metastatic bone disease briefly from an orthopedic-oncology perspective. We synthesized literature identified through PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library, supplemented by targeted verification and updating of cited sources during revision in 2026. Classifications, clinical practice guidelines, clinical trials, cohort studies, and reviews informed the synthesis. Management depends on histological subtype, anatomical site, disease extent, symptoms, and the feasibility of preserving function. Suspected primary bone sarcomas should be imaged locally, staged with chest computed tomography, and referred to a sarcoma center before biopsy. Observation or intralesional treatment is appropriate for many benign lesions, whereas selected locally aggressive tumors require more extensive intervention. Osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma generally require systemic chemotherapy and local treatment. Surgery remains central to conventional chondrosarcoma management, and systemic treatment options differ across its subtypes. Molecular findings support, but do not replace, integrated radiological and histopathological diagnosis. Checkpoint inhibitors have shown limited activity in unselected bone sarcomas, and multikinase inhibitors have modest activity in relapsed osteosarcoma. Patient-specific implants, radiomics, liquid biopsy, and cellular therapies are promising, but each requires prospective evidence of improved patient outcomes before broad adoption. Accurate biopsy planning, specialist pathology review, and coordinated sarcoma care remain essential.

title: Vertebral Fragility in Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance Despite Denosumab: Lessons From a Case.
abstract: Evidence on antiosteoporotic therapies in patients with precursor stages of myeloma remains rare. Denosumab (DMAb) use in this setting is extrapolated from postmenopausal osteoporosis trials. We present an 81-year-old woman with known high-risk IgG/κ monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) who transitioned to low-risk smoldering multiple myeloma (SMM) and developed multiple vertebral fractures while receiving DMAb 60 mg. The patient presented two months after an L4 spontaneous fracture, with severe low back pain impairing mobilization. Ten months earlier, she had sustained an L3 refracture. The fractures occurred at six months post-DMAb injections that were sequentially delayed by approximately seven to 10 weeks, respectively. Her disease had been reclassified as low-risk SMM 18 months earlier (bone marrow plasma cells 15%). At presentation, M-protein (1.93 g/dL) and free light chain (FLC) ratio (5.11) were rising but below the 20/2/20 thresholds. A new lumbar spine CT revealed L1 collapse with vacuum cleft and showed progression of the L4 fracture and the L3 refracture. DMAb was already 10 weeks delayed. S-NTx (13.5 nmBCE) and S-PINP (40.4 ng/mL) were elevated above the median premenopausal values (12.6 nmBCE and 37.5 ng/mL, respectively), consistent with the rebound phenomenon. Given the prolonged DMAb exposure (four years), the delayed timing of the switch (8.5 months after the last dose), and the very high imminent fracture risk, resumption of DMAb was considered preferable to transition to zoledronate. Multilevel percutaneous balloon kyphoplasty was performed at L1, L4, and L3 refracture to reduce pain and preserve or gain height where possible. Intraoperative biopsies were received from L1, L2, and iliac bone. Adjacent fractures with cement, along with poor bone quality, indicated prophylactic cementation of L2. Biopsies confirmed L1 osteonecrosis and showed no evidence of myeloma. Despite the fracture burden and lack of a whole-body MRI, the patient remained under surveillance, since she was classified as having low-to-intermediate risk SMM. Administering DMAb at approximately six months + 6.9 weeks of DMAb delay did not prevent the L3 refracture six months later. Thus, DMAb was given at shortened intervals (three months, then every four months) for one year and was monitored with S-NTx and PINP. This regimen attenuated bone resorption (S-NTx (7.5 to 8.4 nmBCE)) but did not suppress it below the lower premenopausal level before the next injection. PINP decreased below the median premenopausal value after one year of therapy. Post-kyphoplasty, a new L2 superior end plate fracture occurred within six months. At nine-month follow-up, a new bone marrow biopsy showed 10% bone marrow clonal plasma cells (BMPCs), and whole-body low-dose CT was negative for lytic lesions. L1 retropulsion progressed without neurologic symptoms. After three years on DMAb 60 mg every six months, no new fractures or neurologic complications occurred. This case highlights the clinical ambiguity when increasing disease burden in patients with MGUS/SMM overlaps with the DMAb-related rebound phenomenon. Additionally, it underscores the gap in evidence-based treatment strategies for osteoporosis in SMM. Percutaneous kyphoplasty combined with monitored denosumab may be a viable option for patients with MGUS/SMM, very high imminent fracture risk and no neurologic deficits, if intervention is indicated.

title: Amrubicin-Induced Radiation Recall Pneumonitis After Low-Dose Palliative Thoracic Radiotherapy: A Case Report.
abstract: A 70-year-old man with extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer received palliative thoracic radiotherapy to a total dose of 18 Gy in six fractions for central airway stenosis. Five months later, second-line amrubicin was initiated. After two courses of treatment, he was admitted with fever and cough and was initially treated for suspected bacterial pneumonia. Despite cefepime treatment, computed tomography revealed worsening pulmonary opacities corresponding to the previously irradiated field. Bronchoscopy showed no visible endobronchial tumor, cytology revealed no malignant cells, and microbiological studies were negative. Amrubicin-induced radiation recall pneumonitis (RRP) was clinically diagnosed. Amrubicin was discontinued, and oral prednisolone was initiated at 30 mg/day, resulting in rapid clinical and radiographic improvement. Prednisolone was subsequently tapered to 10 mg/day without radiographic worsening at that dose. This case highlights that RRP should be considered after amrubicin therapy, even when the previous thoracic radiation dose was relatively low.

title: Managing Severe Proximal Femoral Fibrous Dysplasia in a Young Adult Using Hemiarthroplasty in a Resource-Constrained Healthcare System: A Case Report.
abstract: Fibrous dysplasia of the proximal femur may lead to progressive deformity, pain, and pathological fractures, with shepherd's crook deformity representing one of its most severe manifestations. Although valgus osteotomy with intramedullary fixation is considered the preferred surgical treatment, extensive bone destruction and limited healthcare resources may preclude conventional reconstruction. We present a case of severe proximal femoral fibrous dysplasia successfully managed with bipolar cemented hemiarthroplasty in a resource-constrained healthcare setting. A 25-year-old man presented with progressive left hip pain, severe proximal femoral deformity, and impaired ambulation. Radiographic evaluation demonstrated lateral bowing of the proximal femur, while histopathological examination following core biopsy confirmed fibrous dysplasia. Internal fixation using an intramedullary nail was initially planned; however, intraoperative findings revealed extensive fibro-osseous replacement, severely compromised bone quality, and inadequate cortical support, making stable fixation technically impossible. Because more complex reconstructive procedures were not covered by the national health insurance system, a bipolar cemented hemiarthroplasty, augmented with plate fixation of the osteotomized fragments, was performed as a salvage procedure. The postoperative course was uneventful, with marked pain relief, improved gait, and satisfactory functional recovery at 10 months of follow-up (Oxford Hip Score 34/48). Conventional fixation for shepherd's crook deformity requires adequate residual cortical bone to achieve stable implant fixation. In cases with extensive cortical destruction and bone stock too thin to support reliable press-fit fixation, cemented hemiarthroplasty may represent a practical alternative. Preservation of the native acetabulum may also reduce postoperative instability while providing satisfactory functional outcomes. Bipolar cemented hemiarthroplasty may be an effective salvage option for selected patients with severe proximal femoral fibrous dysplasia when conventional fixation is technically unfeasible, particularly in resource-constrained healthcare systems.

title: Identification of Noninvasive Biomarkers for Gallbladder Carcinoma.
abstract: Background Carcinoma of the gallbladder (GBC) is an aggressive malignancy of the hepatobiliary system with a poor prognosis due to late presentation and a lack of effective diagnostic tools. Conventional imaging often fails to accurately detect the disease in its early stages. Both abdominal USG and contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) have lower sensitivities for early-stage GBC. This highlights the need for reliable noninvasive biomarkers that may facilitate early diagnosis and improve clinical outcomes. These novel molecular markers may be used alone or in combination with serum tumor markers to enhance their diagnostic utility. This study was performed to identify novel, noninvasive biomarkers for the diagnosis of GBC and determine their accuracy in differentiating carcinoma from other benign pathologies of the gallbladder. Materials and methods This prospective observational case-control study was conducted over a period of one year, from April 2025 to March 2026, in the Department of General Surgery, Motilal Nehru Medical College, Prayagraj. A total of 60 patients were included, comprising 30 histologically confirmed GBC cases and 30 controls with benign gallbladder disease. Detailed clinical evaluations, laboratory investigations, and imaging studies were performed. Blood samples were collected prior to intervention, and biomarkers, including carbohydrate antigen (CA) 19-9, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), and CA-125, were analyzed using ELISA, while microRNA (miRNA)-21 and miRNA-155 were analyzed using quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) techniques. Statistical analysis was performed, and diagnostic accuracy was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Results Patients with GBC showed significantly higher levels of the tumor markers CA 19-9, CEA, and CA-125 compared to controls (p < 0.001). The molecular biomarkers miRNA-21 and miRNA-155 were also markedly elevated in carcinoma cases and strongly correlated with tumor stage and histological grade. The combination of biomarkers (CA 19-9 and miRNA-21) showed superior diagnostic accuracy (91.7%), with higher sensitivity (93.3%) and specificity (90%) on ROC analysis (area under the curve (AUC) of 0.956). Clinical and radiological findings were consistent with advanced disease in most cases. Conclusion Noninvasive biomarkers, particularly when used in combination, demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy for the early detection of GBC. Integration of biomarker analysis with clinical and radiological evaluation can further improve diagnostic utility and facilitate better clinical management. These findings support the potential role of biomarker-based screening strategies in high-risk populations.

title: From Algorithm to Care: AI-Assisted Glaucoma Screening in Real-World Settings.
abstract: Glaucoma screening is increasingly being discussed in the context of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly as imaging technologies become more accessible outside specialist clinics. The question, however, is not simply whether AI can identify a suspicious optic nerve head, but whether it can contribute to a screening pathway that works in real-world clinical settings. Fundus image-based AI has shown promising performance and is now being explored in community and primary eye care. The clinical value of these advances, however, depends on how effectively AI-assisted screening integrates into routine care pathways. Media opacity and poor-quality images can limit assessment, indiscriminate screening can generate unnecessary referrals, and many patients who are identified as requiring further evaluation may not complete the referral pathway. In glaucoma, the value of AI-assisted screening depends on its ability to facilitate appropriate clinical assessment and subsequent care for those identified as being at risk. AI is therefore best considered one part of a screening strategy rather than a replacement for clinical assessment. Risk-based selection, early recognition of ungradable images, and appropriate management of visually significant cataracts or other media opacity may make screening more efficient. Portable or tablet-based visual field testing could add functional assessment at the primary-care level, although its role remains to be established. The next phase of AI-based glaucoma screening should therefore focus less on improving performance metrics in isolation and more on understanding where the technology fits within existing eye-care services. The ultimate measure of success is not the number of suspicious optic nerve heads an algorithm identifies, but whether people with previously undetected glaucoma reach timely diagnosis, treatment, and ongoing care.

title: Age-Associated Variation in Brainstem Anteroposterior Dimensions on 3-Tesla MRI: A Single-Center Study of an Imaging-Normal Clinical Cohort.
abstract: Introduction Brainstem morphometry on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides quantitative information on age-related structural variation. Although previous studies have reported brainstem dimensions in different populations, the relationship between age and anteroposterior (AP) brainstem dimensions remains incompletely characterized in imaging-normal clinical cohorts. This study evaluated age- and sex-related variation in the AP diameters of the midbrain, pons, and medulla in adults undergoing brain MRI. Methods This retrospective cross-sectional study included 140 adults (70 males and 70 females) aged ≥18 years who underwent brain MRI for non-brainstem-related clinical indications and demonstrated no brainstem abnormalities. MRI examinations were performed using a 3.0-Tesla Philips Ingenia MRI system (Philips Medical Systems Nederland B.V., Best, The Netherlands). AP diameters of the midbrain, pons, and medulla were measured on midsagittal T1-weighted images using electronic calipers. Differences between sexes were assessed using independent-samples t-tests, while differences across five age categories (18-30, 31-40, 41-50, 51-60, and >60 years) were assessed using one-way analysis of variance with post-hoc testing. Age was also analyzed as a continuous variable using regression models adjusted for sex. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, Version 25 (Released 2017; IBM Corp., Armonk, New York). Results The mean AP diameters of the midbrain, pons, and medulla were 16.84 ± 1.50 mm, 22.06 ± 1.45 mm, and 12.74 ± 1.06 mm, respectively. No statistically significant sex differences were observed for the midbrain (t(138) = -1.96, p = 0.052), pons (t(138) = 0.15, p = 0.885), or medulla (t(138) = 1.33, p = 0.185), although a marginal trend was observed for the midbrain (p = 0.052). Midbrain AP diameter differed across age categories (F(4,135) = 7.29, p < 0.001, η² = 0.178), with the smallest mean diameter in participants aged >60 years. Post-hoc analysis showed greater midbrain diameters in the 18-30, 31-40, and 41-50-year groups than in the >60-year group. Pons diameter showed an overall age-group difference (F(4,135) = 2.73, p = 0.032, η² = 0.075), but no individual pairwise comparison was statistically significant. Medulla diameter did not differ significantly across age groups (F(4,135) = 0.41, p = 0.803, η² = 0.012). In sex-adjusted continuous-age regression, midbrain AP diameter showed an inverse association with age (β = -0.036 mm/year, t(137) = -5.23, 95% CI: -0.050 to -0.023, p < 0.001), whereas associations were not statistically significant for the pons (β = -0.002 mm/year, t(137) = -0.27, 95% CI: -0.016 to 0.013, p = 0.793) or medulla (β = -0.005 mm/year, t(137) = -0.98, 95% CI: -0.015 to 0.005, p = 0.333). No statistically significant age-by-sex interactions were identified. Conclusions In this single-center study of an imaging-normal clinical cohort, midbrain AP diameter demonstrated an age-associated reduction, whereas the pons and medulla showed no significant linear age association. No statistically significant sex differences or age-by-sex interactions were identified. These findings provide exploratory baseline measurements of brainstem AP dimensions in an imaging-normal clinical cohort and support further investigation using larger multicenter cohorts, standardized MRI protocols, reproducibility assessment, and three-dimensional or automated morphometric approaches.

title: A Rare Case of Primary Renal Liposarcoma.
abstract: Within the broad category of retroperitoneal tumors, primary renal liposarcoma represents an exceedingly rare entity, accounting for less than 1% of tumors. Presentations are often nonspecific, but providers should focus on initial stabilization and consultation with specialists. We present a rare case of primary renal liposarcoma presenting with nonspecific symptoms. A 79-year-old female presented with an abdominal mass, nausea, and bilateral lower extremity edema. Computed tomography (CT) revealed a heterogeneous right retroperitoneal mass measuring 20.6 x 14.9 x 16.0 cm. A subsequent biopsy showed de-differentiated liposarcoma positive for MDM2 (via amplification testing) and CD34 (atypical for this entity). The patient was ultimately discharged and had extensive outpatient resection done. The diagnostic pathway for primary renal liposarcoma begins with a CT, followed by tissue biopsy. Unfortunately, renal liposarcomas carry a poor prognosis because these tumors grow remarkably large due to the ability of the retroperitoneum to accommodate them, and the location itself causes anatomical constraints to surgery. This case highlights that even in the absence of severe clinical complaints, malignant pathology cannot be ruled out. The emergency department (ED) has become an increasingly important pathway for cancer diagnosis, and emergency medicine (EM) physicians play an essential role in initiating multidisciplinary care of patients with aggressive malignancies.

title: Segment-Targeted Resection Strategy for Bilateral Hepatolithiasis: A Retrospective Study in Bangladesh.
abstract: Background Bilateral hepatolithiasis is difficult to treat because stones may be distributed across multiple intrahepatic ducts and may persist despite duct exploration and biliary drainage. We evaluated a segment-targeted surgical strategy designed to remove the hepatic segments most frequently involved in our patients with bilateral hepatolithiasis. Materials and methods We retrospectively reviewed 120 patients who underwent surgery for hepatolithiasis at Bangladesh Medical University, Dhaka, between 2010 and 2024. Forty-six patients had bilateral hepatolithiasis on preoperative magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography, of whom 40 with available follow-up data were included. Patients treated from 2010 to 2020 formed Group I (n = 26) and underwent conventional surgical management consisting of extended choledocholithotomy and/or extrahepatic bile duct excision with biliary reconstruction. Patients treated from 2021 to 2024 formed Group II (n = 14) and underwent combined resection of segments 2, 3, 5, and 6, extrahepatic bile duct excision, irrigation of the remaining intrahepatic ducts, and Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy. Complete stone clearance, residual stones, recurrent postoperative cholangitis, hospital readmission for cholangitis, and postoperative endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) were compared. Results Complete stone clearance was documented in 12 of 26 patients (46.2%) in Group I and 14 of 14 patients (100%) in Group II (Fisher's exact test, p < 0.001). Residual stones were identified in 14 Group I patients (53.8%) and none in Group II. Recurrent postoperative cholangitis requiring hospital readmission occurred in 14 Group I patients (53.8%) and none in Group II. Six Group I patients (23.1%) underwent postoperative ERCP for stone or stent management; no Group II patient required this intervention. Follow-up duration was up to 14 years in Group I and ranged from four months to four years in Group II. Conclusions In this single-center retrospective cohort, segment-targeted resection combined with extrahepatic bile duct excision and Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy was associated with complete stone clearance and no documented recurrent postoperative cholangitis during follow-up. These findings support prospective evaluation of the technique in larger cohorts with standardized follow-up.

title: Melanoma Metastasis to a Pituitary Neuroendocrine Tumor: A Case Report and Literature Review.
abstract: We report a 44-year-old man with a non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma diagnosed approximately 10 years before the current presentation. He subsequently developed metastatic amelanotic melanoma originating from a cutaneous lesion of the right auricle, with jejunal metastases. After disease progression despite immunotherapy and chemotherapy, he presented with visual disturbances and panhypopituitarism. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 28 × 22 × 30 mm endo-suprasellar mass compressing the optic chiasm. The patient underwent endoscopic transnasal transsphenoidal resection. Histopathological and immunohistochemical examination identified two tumors of distinct histogenesis within the same specimen: a pituitary adenoma and metastatic melanoma. The melanoma component was positive for Melan-A, HMB-45, SOX10, and S-100, confirming melanoma metastasis to the pituitary adenoma and establishing tumor-to-tumor metastasis. Postoperatively, the patient's visual function improved, and he was discharged on postoperative Day 5. This case demonstrates the diagnostic value of thorough histopathological and immunohistochemical evaluation when the clinical behavior of a previously diagnosed sellar lesion changes in a patient with systemic malignancy. Surgical decompression improved visual function and provided a definitive tissue diagnosis, supporting coordinated multidisciplinary management.

title: Symptomatic Post-anastomotic Blind Ileal Pouch.
abstract: Postsurgical blind pouch syndrome is an uncommon late complication of intestinal reconstruction caused by stasis within a poorly emptying bowel segment. Its manifestations range from chronic diarrhea and abdominal discomfort to bleeding, obstruction, inflammation, and perforation, while diagnosis may be difficult when the previous operative anatomy is unknown. We report the case of a 48-year-old man who presented with severe right-sided abdominal pain, distension, and peritoneal irritation three years after emergency bowel resection and an undocumented intestinal anastomosis following a motor vehicle collision. Since the previous operation, he had experienced frequent bowel movements and fecal urgency that substantially impaired his quality of life. Initial computed tomography and diagnostic laparoscopy failed to identify a definitive cause of his symptoms, and extensive adhesions prevented complete characterization of the reconstruction. Persistent severe pain, fever, and marked elevation of inflammatory markers prompted repeat exploration five days later. Laparotomy demonstrated a patent side-to-side ileocecal anastomosis associated with a markedly dilated and thickened blind ileal pouch and a separate atrophic terminal ileal remnant. The blind pouch was resected. Histopathological examination revealed superficial mucosal ulceration, muscular hypertrophy, edema, hemorrhage, focal liquefactive necrosis, and acute-on-chronic transmural inflammation without malignancy. Recovery was uneventful. At three-month follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic and medication-free, with normal bowel function and complete resolution of fecal urgency and abdominal pain. This case highlights that a postsurgical blind ileal pouch may cause severe acute inflammation even without gross perforation and should be considered in patients with unexplained abdominal symptoms after intestinal reconstruction.

title: Fluoroscopy-Assisted Transcervical Removal of a Retained Grill-Brush Bristle: A Case Report.
abstract: Retained grill-brush bristles can be difficult to localize and remove when embedded in cervical soft tissues. The present case report highlights the role of fluoroscopy-assisted transcervical exploration following unsuccessful transoral retrieval. Dye diffusion limited the usefulness of computed tomography (CT)-guided India ink marking, while differences in head position compromised the reliability of CT-based surgical navigation. Removal was achieved through a lateral cervicotomy using C-arm fluoroscopy and clips as radiopaque reference markers, followed by an uneventful recovery. This case illustrates the importance of combining adequate surgical access with reliable intraoperative localization when a deeply embedded cervical bristle cannot be retrieved transorally.

title: Biliary Myeloid Sarcoma Mimicking Cholangiocarcinoma: A Diagnostic Pitfall.
abstract: A 53-year-old man presented with a three-day history of jaundice and anorexia. Laboratory tests showed markedly elevated liver enzymes and bilirubin, consistent with obstructive jaundice. Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) demonstrated marked thickening and enhancement of the extrahepatic bile duct from the hepatic confluence to the ampulla, with intrahepatic ductal dilatation and no clear involvement of the right or left hepatic ducts. Hilar cholangiocarcinoma (Bismuth-Corlette type II) was strongly suspected, and a multidisciplinary tumor board proposed an extended left hepatectomy with bile duct resection. The patient first underwent percutaneous biliary drainage and left portal vein embolization. Intraoperative biopsies of the right and left hepatic ducts showed no evidence of adenocarcinoma, and surgery was completed without complications. Final pathology revealed myeloid sarcoma of the extrahepatic bile ducts, with architectural effacement by a diffuse proliferation of intermediate-sized cells with scant cytoplasm and monotonous round nuclei. The cells were diffusely positive for myeloperoxidase and multifocally positive for CD117, and negative for pancytokeratin, B-cell markers, T-cell markers, CD138, CD34, and CD163, excluding an epithelial neoplasm and lymphoma. Bone marrow involvement was subsequently identified, and the patient is awaiting chemotherapy followed by allogeneic stem cell transplantation. Many inflammatory and neoplastic biliary conditions mimic cholangiocarcinoma on imaging. Biopsy or cytology is therefore recommended before surgery. Myeloid sarcoma, a tumor of extramedullary myeloid blasts, is equivalent to a diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia. Primary biliary involvement is exceedingly rare and may be misdiagnosed as cholangitis or cholangiocarcinoma.

title: A Case Report of Intraoperative Shock Following Spinal Anesthesia: Could It Be All of the Above?
abstract: Perioperative cardiovascular collapse may result from several life-threatening conditions with overlapping clinical manifestations, making the diagnosis challenging. We present a case of a 37-year-old man with morbid obesity who underwent fixation of a tibial plateau fracture. Following an uneventful ultrasound-guided femoral nerve block and spinal anesthesia, intravenous cefazolin was administered. Within minutes, the patient developed lightheadedness, nausea, loss of consciousness, jaw rigidity, and severe hypotension, refractory to fluid administration and vasopressor boluses, followed by bradycardia and respiratory distress. Point-of-care echocardiography showed preserved biventricular function and findings suggestive of marked hypovolemia, without right ventricular dysfunction. One hour after hemodynamic stabilization, the patient developed a maculopapular rash. Serial serum tryptase concentrations were markedly elevated, supporting the diagnosis of perioperative anaphylaxis. The patient recovered uneventfully and was referred to an allergy and immunology specialist. This case highlights the complexity of diagnosing sudden cardiovascular collapse during neuraxial anesthesia when several potentially life-threatening conditions are considered. Perioperative anaphylaxis should always be considered in cases of unexplained severe hypotension, even in the absence of bronchospasm or cutaneous manifestations.

title: Local Radiotherapy and Androgen Deprivation Therapy (ADT) Monotherapy for Low-Volume Metastatic Hormone-Sensitive Prostate Cancer: Real-World Outcomes in the Era of PSMA PET-CT Staging.
abstract: Background Randomized trials established the survival benefit of primary tumor radiotherapy (RT) in low-volume metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (mHSPC), typically alongside upfront docetaxel or androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPI). However, in real-world practice, systemic intensification is frequently omitted due to age, comorbidities, or cost. In parallel, diagnostic imaging has shifted from conventional CT and bone scan to PSMA PET-CT. We hypothesized that patients with low metastatic burden accurately staged via highly sensitive PSMA PET-CT can achieve durable survival with prostate RT and androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) alone. Methods We retrospectively reviewed patients with newly diagnosed, PSMA PET-CT-staged, low-volume mHSPC treated at a single center between January 2019 and April 2025. All received high-dose prostate RT and continuous ADT monotherapy. Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. Univariate and multivariate Cox regression models were utilized to identify prognostic factors for PFS. Results Fifty patients were identified. The most common radiotherapy fractionation was 55 Gy in 20 fractions (n=45, 90%). At a median follow-up duration of 31 months, median PFS and OS were not reached. The two-year OS and PFS were 96% and 82%, respectively. On univariate analysis, favorable prognostic factors included non-T4 stage, low PSA at six months post-RT, PSA <0.2 ng/mL at six months post-RT, and low absolute PSA nadir. PSA <0.2 ng/mL at six months post-RT remained as a significant prognostic factor in multivariate analysis. The two-year PFS for patients achieving a PSA <0.2 ng/mL at six months was higher than those with PSA ≥ 0.2 ng/mL (96% vs. 61%, HR 0.07, 95% CI 0.01-0.57, p=0.013). Conclusion While upfront systemic treatment intensification remains the current standard of care for mHSPC, for patients with low-volume disease staged by PSMA PET-CT who cannot receive or tolerate upfront systemic intensification, preliminary data show pairing prostate RT with ADT monotherapy still achieves favorable PFS and OS, and is an explorable alternative that should be validated by prospective studies. A six-month post-RT PSA threshold of <0.2 ng/mL is a significant prognostic factor for PFS and could be explored for its utility in identifying candidates for continued de-escalated therapy versus those requiring timely systemic re-intensification.

title: Phyllodes Tumors of the Breast in 2026: A Contemporary Narrative Review of Diagnosis, Surgical Margins, Prognosis, and Emerging Therapies.
abstract: Phyllodes tumors of the breast are rare fibroepithelial neoplasms characterized by significant heterogeneity regarding morphology, biological behavior, and clinical outcome. This review summarizes current developments in the diagnosis, histopathological and molecular classification, therapeutic management, and emerging technologies associated with phyllodes tumors of the breast. A literature search was conducted across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Embase, and Google Scholar, focusing on publications from the 2000-2026 period. The literature search covered publications from January 1, 2000, to September 30, 2026, and was last updated on September 30, 2026. Mammography, ultrasound, and magnetic resonance imaging contribute to preoperative assessment, although significant diagnostic overlap with fibroadenomas persists. Core needle biopsy is a key diagnostic tool, yet lesion heterogeneity can limit the accuracy of histological classification. Advances in molecular pathology have identified mutations and pathways associated with the progression and aggressiveness of phyllodes tumors, though these have not yet replaced morphological assessment. Surgical excision with negative margins remains the primary therapeutic approach, while the risk of local recurrence depends on histological grade, surgical margins, and other clinicopathological characteristics. Radiotherapy in phyllodes tumors of the breast appears to offer benefits primarily regarding local control in selected high-risk cases. Emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, radiomics, and digital pathology, are proving to be promising tools for diagnosis, grading, and prognostic assessment. Overall, modern management of phyllodes tumors of the breast is shifting toward more personalized and multifactorial approaches.

title: When Appearances Deceive: A Silent Somatotroph Macroadenoma Presenting With Acromegaloid Features and Paradoxically Low Insulin-Like Growth Factor-1.
abstract: Silent somatotroph adenomas are uncommon pituitary neuroendocrine tumours (PitNETs) of the PIT1 lineage that express growth hormone (GH) immunohistochemically but without biochemical evidence of acromegaly. We report the case of a 32-year-old male patient referred with recurrent epistaxis, headache, right-sided diplopia, and third cranial nerve palsy. Clinical examination revealed acromegaloid features including frontal bossing, spade-like hands, and coarse facies, which were strongly suggestive of longstanding GH excess. However, preoperative insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1) was paradoxically low at 13.1 nmol/L (reference range 15.5-33.1 nmol/L), creating a striking clinical-biochemical discordance. MRI demonstrated a giant sellar and suprasellar mass with chiasmal compression, right cavernous sinus invasion, and extension into the paranasal sinuses. The patient underwent endoscopic transsphenoidal resection. Neuropathology confirmed a densely granulated PIT1-lineage somatotroph adenoma with scattered GH positivity, diffuse Pit-1 staining, and a Ki-67 index below 2%. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge posed by silent somatotroph adenomas, underscores the limitations of biochemical assessment alone, and reinforces the essential role of histopathology and immunohistochemistry in establishing a definitive diagnosis. Long-term endocrine and neurosurgical surveillance is strongly recommended given the potential for phenotypic transformation to a functioning acromegaly syndrome.

title: Congenital Cervical Vertebral Segmentation Failure Presenting as Refractory Torticollis in Infancy: A Case of Klippel-Feil Syndrome.
abstract: We present a case of a six-month-old female with a five-month history of right-sided torticollis that showed little improvement despite physical therapy. She presented to the emergency department due to parental concern for pneumonia, with congestion and cough without respiratory distress. Physical examination demonstrated leftward rotation and right lateral flexion of the head and cervical spine, consistent with the previously diagnosed right-sided torticollis. Chest radiographs were obtained in the workup for pneumonia and incidentally revealed segmentation anomalies of the cervical and upper thoracic spine as well as multiple bilateral bifid and fused ribs, more pronounced on the right. The radiographic findings were interpreted as highly suggestive of Klippel-Feil syndrome (KFS). In the setting of refractory torticollis and characteristic congenital vertebral abnormalities, the diagnosis of KFS was made. No acute complication requiring immediate intervention was documented. Referral to appropriate specialists was recommended for further evaluation and longitudinal management. This case highlights the importance of maintaining a broad differential diagnosis when evaluating refractory torticollis in infancy. In this patient, congenital vertebral segmentation abnormalities were identified incidentally on imaging obtained during evaluation for an unrelated respiratory concern. Recognition of these abnormalities led to the diagnosis of KFS and referral for further specialist evaluation.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Preoperative High-Resolution Computed Tomography Compared With Intraoperative Findings in Active Squamous Chronic Otitis Media: A Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: Background and objective High-resolution CT (HRCT) is widely used to map cholesteatoma before surgery, but its diagnostic performance differs across temporal bone structures. This study evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of preoperative HRCT and used paired analysis to determine whether HRCT systematically over- or underdetected operative findings in active squamous chronic otitis media. Methods This cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study included 55 patients who underwent temporal bone HRCT followed by cholesteatoma surgery at Bangladesh Medical University from September 1, 2025, to August 29, 2026. Intraoperative findings were the reference standard. Patient-level 2 × 2 tables were used to calculate sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), and overall accuracy with exact 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Two-sided exact McNemar tests were used for paired comparisons, with Holm adjustment as a multiplicity sensitivity analysis. Results The mean age of the cohort was 23.02 ± 11.33 years, and 39/55 patients (70.9%) were male. Scutum erosion was present in 55/55 patients (100.0%) on both HRCT and surgery. Overall accuracy was 52/55 (94.5%) for posterior meatal wall erosion and 51/55 (92.7%) for lateral semicircular canal (LSCC) fistula. Incus erosion was detected in 37/55 patients (67.3%) on HRCT and 50/55 (90.9%) at surgery; sensitivity was 36/50 (72.0%) and specificity 4/5 (80.0%) (exact McNemar p = 0.00098; Holm-adjusted p = 0.0049). Tegmen erosion was reported in 28/55 patients (50.9%) on HRCT versus 4/55 (7.3%) at surgery, and facial canal dehiscence in 38/55 (69.1%) versus 11/55 (20.0%); both were significantly overdetected and remained significant after Holm adjustment. Mesotympanic involvement was 48/55 (87.3%) on HRCT versus 39/55 (70.9%) at surgery (p = 0.035), but no disease-extension comparison remained significant after Holm adjustment. Conclusions HRCT is a useful preoperative surgical roadmap in cholesteatoma, but its diagnostic performance is structure-dependent. It performed well for posterior meatal wall erosion and lateral semicircular canal fistula, while incus erosion was significantly underdetected and tegmen erosion and facial canal dehiscence were significantly overdetected. Exact McNemar analysis appropriately accounts for the paired nature of HRCT and intraoperative observations and should be interpreted alongside structure-specific diagnostic accuracy measures.

title: Ovarian Myxoma in a Patient With Missed Abortion: A Diagnostic Dilemma.
abstract: Ovarian myxoma is a rare benign mesenchymal tumor. It can be completely asymptomatic and is difficult to differentiate from other ovarian masses before surgery and final histopathology. We report a case of a 28-year-old primigravida who presented with a missed abortion at 11 weeks. Transvaginal ultrasonography incidentally showed a 6.5 × 5.7 cm complex solid-cystic right adnexal lesion in the pouch of Douglas. She was asymptomatic from the mass. After dilatation and evacuation for missed abortion, the patient was evaluated for an ovarian mass, and tumor markers were found negative. Repeat ultrasonography showed a heterogeneous lesion with coarse hyperechoic foci and posterior acoustic shadowing, suggesting a right ovarian teratoma. The patient was taken for laparotomy, wherein an 8 × 8 cm solid-cystic mass was found in the right ovary, and right ovarian cystectomy was done. Intraoperative scrape cytology came back negative for malignancy and showed columnar cells, squamous cells, and mature adipose tissue, which favored a benign cystic teratoma. Histopathology showed a thick collagenous capsule and stellate cells in abundant myxoid stroma without atypia. On immunohistochemistry, the tumor cells were positive for vimentin and negative for desmin and cytokeratin. The final diagnosis was ovarian myxoma. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. There was no recurrence at one-year follow-up. This case shows that ovarian myxoma can mimic a mature cystic teratoma on imaging, gross examination, and cytology, and that the final diagnosis depends on histopathological examination (HPE) supported by immunohistochemistry.

title: Diffuse-Type Tenosynovial Giant Cell Tumor of the Flexor Hallucis Longus Tendon Sheath: A Case Report.
abstract: The synovium can be the primary site for the development of various benign or malignant tumors. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT), also known as giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath, is a benign but locally aggressive synovial neoplasm occurring in localized and diffuse forms. The localized form predominantly affects the hand, whereas the diffuse form mainly involves large joints; involvement of the flexor hallucis longus tendon sheath is rare. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the principal modality for demonstrating the hemosiderin deposits characteristic of this lesion, although histopathology remains necessary for definitive diagnosis. Surgical resection remains the standard treatment. We report the case of a 24-year-old man with 10 months of right ankle pain, related to a diffuse-type TGCT involving the flexor hallucis longus tendon sheath and adjacent ankle joints. Radiographs initially showed soft-tissue filling of Kager's triangle. Computed tomography arthrography demonstrated synovial thickening but was nonspecific; MRI then revealed the characteristic findings, and histopathology confirmed the diagnosis. This report aims to raise awareness of this rare location and its associated diagnostic pitfalls.

title: Congenital Hypoplasia of the C1 Posterior Arch Masquerading as Multiple Sclerosis: A Case Report.
abstract: Hypoplasia of the C1 posterior arch is a rare congenital anomaly, classified using the Currarino system into subtypes A through E depending on the extent and nature of arch deficiency. The majority of cases are incidental radiological findings; symptomatic presentations causing cervical myelopathy are exceptionally uncommon and not well represented in the surgical literature. In such cases, the absence of established management guidelines renders clinical decision-making particularly challenging. We present a case of a 45-year-old male surgeon who presented with a one-year history of episodic bilateral upper and lower limb weakness. Initial investigations, including brain and cervical spine MRI, were interpreted as consistent with a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, for which treatment was commenced. Following a symptom-free interval after a one-month course of corticosteroids, the patient experienced a recurrence at eight months, prompting dynamic MRI of the cervical spine, which revealed a type C hypoplastic C1 posterior arch causing dynamic spinal cord compression during hyperextension. The diagnosis was revised accordingly. Supplementary investigations confirmed atlantoaxial stability and normal vertebral artery anatomy bilaterally. The patient provided consent and underwent posterior surgical decompression of the entire posterior arch, without instrumented fusion. Intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring guided the extent of resection; decompression began on the fibrous left-sided arch, extending to the level of the vertebral artery groove, followed by the bony right-sided arch, sequenced to preserve facet joint integrity. The patient achieved complete symptom resolution postoperatively. This case highlights the diagnostic challenge posed by symptomatic C1 arch hypoplasia, which may mimic demyelinating disease, and demonstrates that surgical decompression, guided by intraoperative neurophysiological monitoring and tailored to arch morphology, can achieve excellent neurological outcomes without the need for instrumented stabilisation.

title: Diagnostic Tools Used for Tuberculous Pleural Effusion and Their Association With Treatment Outcomes.
abstract: Background Tuberculous pleural effusion (TPE) is difficult to confirm because pleural disease is often paucibacillary. Pleural-fluid biomarkers, culture, molecular assays, and pleural biopsy can improve diagnostic certainty, but their availability varies substantially in resource-limited settings. Objective To describe the diagnostic investigations used for suspected TPE at AlShaab and Abu Anjaa Teaching Hospitals in Khartoum, Sudan, from February to July 2017, and assess their association with treatment outcomes. Methodology This retrospective cohort study included 69 patients with a clinician-recorded diagnosis of TPE at two teaching hospitals in Khartoum, Sudan, from February to July 2017. The first author collected demographic, clinical, investigation, treatment, and outcome data from patient records using a standardized data-collection checklist. Investigations were classified according to whether a test and result were documented. Associations with outcome were assessed using Fisher's exact test and odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results Chest radiography was performed in 67/69 patients (97.1%). Pleural-fluid adenosine deaminase (ADA) was recorded in 1/69 (1.4%), culture in 6/69 (8.7%), polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in 4/69 (5.8%), and pleural biopsy in 7/69 (10.1%). GeneXpert MTB/RIF (Cepheid, Sunnyvale, CA) and pleural-fluid interferon-gamma testing were not performed. HIV testing was not documented in 50/69 patients (72.5%). Thirteen patients (18.8%) received antituberculous treatment without pleural-fluid or tissue testing. Five (38.5%) had a favorable outcome, and eight (61.5%) had an unfavorable outcome, including four subsequently diagnosed with malignant effusion and one death. Among 56 patients who underwent at least one pleural-fluid or tissue test, 39 (69.6%) had a favorable outcome. Any diagnostic testing was associated with higher odds of favorable outcome (OR 3.67, 95% CI 1.05-12.87; Fisher's exact P = 0.054), although the association did not cross the conventional statistical-significance threshold. Conclusions Confirmatory testing for suspected TPE was used inconsistently, while several clinically useful tests were rarely or never available. Patients treated without pleural-fluid or tissue testing had more unfavorable outcomes, including missed malignant effusion. The findings support a pragmatic minimum diagnostic bundle before prolonged empiric treatment, while recognizing that this observational study cannot establish that testing caused better outcomes.

title: A Case of Advanced Basal Cell Carcinoma of the Head and Neck: Diagnostic Challenges and Sequential Systemic Therapy.
abstract: Advanced cutaneous malignancies with basaloid morphology can present diagnostic and therapeutic challenges, particularly when pathological interpretations differ and disease progresses during systemic treatment. We describe the clinical course of a 53-year-old woman with an extensive, unresectable cutaneous tumor involving the posterior neck and occipital region, accompanied by bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and additional clinically suspected cutaneous deposits. The initial diagnosis was trichoblastic carcinoma, whereas expert pathological review favored basal cell carcinoma. The extent of disease precluded surgery and definitive radiotherapy. First-line vismodegib was initiated, and palliative radiotherapy delivering 30 Gy in 10 fractions to the occipital lesions and bilateral cervical lymph nodes was completed one year later. Clinical progression was documented three months after completion of radiotherapy; one month after this, MRI demonstrated extensive infiltration involving the left parotid gland and adjacent pharyngeal spaces. Second-line cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil were subsequently administered. Follow-up MRI six months after the earlier MRI demonstrated substantial tumor volume reduction. PET/CT three months later showed a heterogeneous response compared with a year earlier, including regression at several previously involved sites and newly apparent metabolically active right axillary lymph nodes. A subsequent biopsy was reported as basaloid carcinoma. The patient later experienced clinical deterioration, received one cycle of cemiplimab, and died before further treatment or response assessment. This case illustrates the importance of pathological clarification, longitudinal imaging, and careful interpretation of treatment response during sequential systemic therapy for advanced basal cell carcinoma.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Computed Tomography for Radiographically Occult Scaphoid Fractures and Concordance With Magnetic Resonance Imaging: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Scaphoid fractures are the most common carpal bone fracture. Non-union and avascular necrosis are complications of a missed fracture. Therefore, if plain radiographs are normal and symptoms persist, further imaging such as computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are often performed. Previous systematic reviews have largely compared their diagnostic accuracy indirectly using separate patient cohorts. Our objective is to determine the diagnostic accuracy of CT for occult scaphoid fractures in patients who underwent both CT and MRI following a negative or equivocal initial radiograph, and to assess concordance between CT and MRI findings. A systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. OVID MEDLINE, OVID Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched for studies published from inception up to August 31, 2026. Eligible studies enrolled adults with clinically suspected scaphoid fracture and a negative or equivocal initial radiograph who subsequently underwent both CT and MRI. Risk of bias was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2). Studies affected by partial verification or incorporation bias were excluded from quantitative synthesis. CT sensitivity and specificity were pooled using a bivariate random-effects model. Concordance between CT and MRI was reported using percentage agreement and Cohen's kappa. Eight studies met the inclusion criteria. Six studies contributed to the primary pooled analysis of CT diagnostic accuracy, with one study reporting two CT readers. Using the first reader data from that study, alongside the five other studies, pooled CT sensitivity was 79% (95% CI 61.5-89.8%) and specificity was 94.4% (95% CI 82.1-98.4%). A sensitivity analysis using the second reader produced a sensitivity of 69.2% (95% CI 48.0-84.6%), with an unchanged specificity of 94.4% (95% CI 85.5-98.0%). Three studies provided CT-MRI concordance data; two demonstrated almost perfect agreement, with Cohen's kappa values of 0.91. The dual-energy CT study demonstrated lower concordance. Three studies used a reference standard independent of both CT and MRI and demonstrated mixed comparative findings. Overall, one study was judged to have low risk of bias, and seven were high risk of bias. In the included studies, CT demonstrated high specificity but more limited sensitivity for occult scaphoid fracture in paired CT-MRI cohorts. These findings align with existing literature reviewing unpaired data sets. Therefore, the findings suggest that CT remains a relevant alternative to MRI, especially in centres where MRI is unavailable or contraindicated, or for surgical planning.
